Reproducing Choi et al. (2025) from dandiset 002014¶

Paper. Choi J, Amjad U, Murray R, Shrivastav R, Teichert T, Goodell B, Olson M, Schaeffer DJ, Oluoch JK, Schwerdt HN (2025). Aseptic, semi-sealed cranial chamber implants for chronic multi-channel neurochemical and electrophysiological neural recording in nonhuman primates. Journal of Neuroscience Methods 420, 110467. doi:10.1016/j.jneumeth.2025.110467. This attempt used the full text of the author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC13250822, CC BY).

Dandiset. DANDI:002014, version 0.261012.0921. The paper cites no DANDI version; its data statement points to a Zenodo record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.14825992), which the dandiset says it includes together with the raw recordings. 0.261012.0921 is the only published version, and the draft holds the same file (same blob) and the same metadata, so the choice changes nothing the analysis uses.

What the dandiset holds. One NWB file: one session (09/27/2024) of monkey T, the session of Figures 8 and 9. Monkey J, and the surgical, culture, drainage and electrode-yield results that make up most of the paper, are not in it.

Outside input. The paper's trial lists in the Zenodo record (successful large and small reward trials) are used only to check the trial selection built here from the dandiset's events.

Code read. The paper links no analysis code. The dandiset links its conversion code, catalystneuro/schwerdt-lab-to-nwb at commit 6edf72904a64d92f3b6d9268d38a31ffab95f36e (choi_2025 and the interfaces it uses). It sets the layout of the trial-aligned FSCV table (60 s rows centred on the trial-start event), rebuilds the LFP from 60 s trial pieces placed by the trial times, places the raw ephys by a starting time of 0 and a rate, and places the raw FSCV by a single starting time.

Data check¶

Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output.

One NWB file, one session (09/27/2024) of monkey T, the session of Figures 8 and 9. Monkey J is not in the dandiset. The subject description ("Two adult female rhesus monkeys were used for in vivo validation of the s-µIP device"), the session and experiment descriptions and the keyword "micro-invasive neural implant" describe micro-invasive probes, the subject of another paper by the lab (the conversion code's amjad_2025 project); they do not describe this paper's chamber. The related publication is this paper. The electrode sites (c7b, c5c, c5d for ephys, c8ds for FSCV) are those of Figures 8 and 9.

The raw ephys has no timestamps: it starts at 0 s, at 32 kHz, so it covers 0 to about 18336 s from the session start. The LFP, the FSCV series, the trials and the events cover about 11825 to 31535 s. The two ranges overlap only in part; the clock checks below deal with this.

# The paper's trial lists on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.14825992), 1-based trial ids.
ZENODO = "https://zenodo.org/api/records/14825992/files/"
lists = {}
for size, name in (("large", "big"), ("small", "small")):
    url = ZENODO + urllib.request.quote(f"09272024_nlx_c8c_value object start_{name} rew and success_tr1-1411.mat") + "/content"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as r:
        lists[size] = set(sio.loadmat(io.BytesIO(r.read()))["trids_out"].ravel().tolist())
for size in ("large", "small"):
    mine = set(succ.trial[succ.reward == size])
    print(f"{size}: Zenodo list {len(lists[size])} trials, dandiset events {len(mine)}, both {len(mine & lists[size])}, "
          f"only in the dandiset {sorted(mine - lists[size])}, only in the list {sorted(lists[size] - mine)}")
print("Last trial:", trials.iloc[-1][["trial", "reward", "error", "trial_start", "stop_time"]].to_dict(),
      "; last LFP sample", round(lfp_t[-1], 3))

large: Zenodo list 451 trials, dandiset events 452, both 451, only in the dandiset [1411], only in the list []
small: Zenodo list 499 trials, dandiset events 499, both 499, only in the dandiset [], only in the list []
Last trial: {'trial': 1411, 'reward': 'large', 'error': nan, 'trial_start': 29938.681817, 'stop_time': 29968.681817} ; last LFP sample 29968.682

The event table stores each event once per trial window that contains it (60 s windows overlap), so labels hold about five copies of each event (7221 stored trial-start events for 1412 distinct ones) and are not sorted; repeats are removed here. After that there are 1412 trial-start events for 1411 trials, and every trial's midpoint_time is one of them. The trial tags are all "initial cue display" and carry no trial type; reward size and outcome come from the events. Every trial has at most one V.

Built from the events, the successful trials match the paper's Zenodo lists exactly (499 small; 451 large) except trial 1411, the last, which the events give as a successful large trial and the list leaves out. Its window runs to the end of the LFP. Trial 1411 is kept here, as the dandiset's events mark it successful; the difference is one trial in 452, and the fig8b section shows the result without it. The list files are named "c8c" while the FSCV site is c8ds (also in the Zenodo record's own FSCV file name). The record describes the lists as trial ids of the session, used for all its neural data sets, so the site in their file names does not bear on which trials they select.

The paper describes the reward size as depending on whether the target is at the top or bottom of the screen; the events code left and right conditions, and both sizes occur on both sides. The dandiset's description also speaks of left and right targets. The data do not say which is right.

The trial-aligned FSCV table has a row for every trial, all marked good, each 601 samples at 10 Hz from 30 s before to 30 s after the trial start. Its columns state no units. The dopamine values (about -54 to 42) fit nM, the unit of Δ[DA] in the lab's earlier work, but the file does not say so. NaN gaps occur in most rows.

The table "bipolar_lfp_series" is described as beta-band LFP. Its spectrum is broadband, falling from 1 Hz up, like the raw c7b minus c5c difference, with the line-noise band (58 to 62 Hz) removed (the Zenodo record speaks of spectral interpolation). Its values are already in volts (at 1 to 4 Hz its density matches the raw difference in volts), but the series carries the raw int16 conversion factor (3.05e-8), so a reader that applies it gets values about 3e7 times too small. Beta power is computed here from the stored values with a band-pass filter, as set in the claims file.

# Dopamine is referenced at V. Where the sample at V is NaN, `reference_at` interpolates between the
# nearest valid samples on each side. Check on a linear ramp with a NaN gap at every position of V
# relative to the 10 Hz grid: the referenced trace must be 0 at V.
worst = 0.0
for phase in np.linspace(0, 0.1, 101):
    t_syn = np.arange(-30, 30.01, 0.1) + phase
    for t0 in (phase, phase + 0.03, phase + 0.05, 0.0):
        ramp = 2 * t_syn
        ramp[np.abs(t_syn - t0) < 0.06] = np.nan
        ref = chamber.reference_at(ramp, t_syn, t0)
        worst = max(worst, np.nanmax(np.abs(ref - 2 * (t_syn - t0))))
print(f"Synthetic ramp: largest error of the reference {worst:.2e}")
assert worst < 1e-9
on_nan = sum(np.isnan(np.interp(row.V, row.trial_start + fscv["t_rel_start"], fscv["da"][row.trial - 1])) for row in succ.itertuples())
print("Successful trials whose dopamine is NaN at V (reference interpolated across the gap, or trial dropped):", int(on_nan), "of", len(succ))

Synthetic ramp: largest error of the reference 3.55e-15
Successful trials whose dopamine is NaN at V (reference interpolated across the gap, or trial dropped): 62 of 951

The reference at V is exact on the synthetic ramp at every position of V on the 10 Hz grid. In 62 of the 951 successful trials dopamine is NaN at V, and none of them has a valid sample within 0.2 s on both sides, so these trials have no reference and drop out of the dopamine claims (889 trials remain in fig8a, and 23 large and 39 small trials are dropped in fig8b).

# Spikes: the thresholded table (the paper's Zenodo file) and the Plexon unit.
g = f["processing/ecephys/thresholded_units"]
print("Thresholded table description:", g.attrs["description"])
print("Electrodes of its units:", g["electrodes"][()].tolist())
for name, st in thr.items():
    print(f"  thresholded unit {name}: {len(st)} spikes, {st.min():.3f} to {st.max():.3f} s, sorted {bool(np.all(np.diff(st) >= 0))}")
for name, st in plx.items():
    print(f"  Plexon unit {name}: {len(st)} spikes, {st.min():.3f} to {st.max():.3f} s, "
          f"sorted {bool(np.all(np.diff(st) >= 0))}, decreasing steps {int(np.sum(np.diff(st) < 0))}")
main_unit = max(thr, key=lambda k: len(thr[k]))
spk = thr[main_unit]
plx_spk = np.sort(next(iter(plx.values())))
nearest = np.minimum(np.abs(spk[np.clip(np.searchsorted(spk, plx_spk), 0, len(spk) - 1)] - plx_spk),
                     np.abs(spk[np.clip(np.searchsorted(spk, plx_spk) - 1, 0, len(spk) - 1)] - plx_spk))
print(f"Plexon spikes within 0.2 ms of a spike of thresholded unit {main_unit}: {np.sum(nearest < 2e-4)} of {len(plx_spk)}; "
      f"within 1 us: {np.sum(nearest < 1e-6)}")
wf = chamber.thresholded_waveforms(f, list(thr).index(main_unit), max_spikes=20000)
print(f"Waveforms: {wf.shape[1]} samples; unit attribute '{g['waveforms'].attrs['unit']}'; mean waveform {wf.mean(0).min():.1f} to "
      f"{wf.mean(0).max():.1f} as stored; fraction of spikes whose largest |value| exceeds 40: {np.mean(np.abs(wf).max(1) > 40):.3f}")
print("Datasets: waveforms", g["waveforms"].shape, ", waveforms_index", g["waveforms_index"].shape, ", spike_times",

The thresholded table holds unit "0" with 3 spikes and unit "1" with the rest; the description says -1 marks poor-quality spikes, and no -1 occurs. Unit 1 is used below. The Plexon unit is a different sorting of the same channel: part of its spikes coincide with unit 1's (counts above), and its spike times are stored out of order. The waveforms are stated in volts, but their values (a mean trough of about -53 over the first 20000 spikes) are microvolts: in all 101733 spikes the largest absolute value exceeds 40 (the smallest is 40.3, printed in the fig9bc section), which fits the 40 µV threshold in the name of the paper's Zenodo file (csc23_100_40uv.mat). Spike times run from 0 to the end of the raw ephys, which suggests the raw ephys clock; the next cell checks this.

The raw ephys on the trial clock runs from 2024-09-27 12:06:44.113006-04:00 to 2024-09-27 17:12:20.102974750-04:00
Header open-to-close span 22952 s; raw samples 18336 s

The raw ephys is found in the stored LFP at a constant offset: raw time 0 is 11812.1 s on the trial clock. The first search covers the whole LFP; the eight checks across the session each find the same offset, to within a few ms that grow steadily with time (the drift printed above), with correlations near 1 against at most about 0.35 elsewhere in the window. The raw search was restricted to 60 s around the candidate at those points because raw c5c sits at the ±1 mV input range in about 1.7% of samples and the raw difference carries a large 10 Hz artefact (the FSCV scan rate), which the stored LFP does not. In one 300 s segment (1633 spikes), raw c5d shows a spike about 7 ms before the stored spike times: the spike-triggered trough is at -7.1 ms, the per-spike troughs lie between -7.4 and -6.9 ms from the 10th to the 90th percentile, and 98.8% lie within 0.5 ms of -7.1 ms. Moving the spike times by 50 to 500 ms removes it, and the other two sites do not show it. So the spike times are on the raw ephys clock, 7 ms late. The 7 ms is small next to the 100 ms bins used below and is left as stored. The raw ephys and the spikes therefore do not share the clock of the trials, events, LFP and FSCV table: as stored they are 11812.1 s early. The file puts the raw ephys at 0 s (it stores a starting time and a rate, no timestamps), and its spike times are counted from the start of the raw samples.

The absolute times do not fit together either. The Neuralynx header gives the recording as opened at the session start (08:49:52) and closed at 15:12:24, a span of about 22950 s, but there are 18336 s of samples. On the trial clock the raw samples end at 17:12:20, two hours after the header's closing time. The data cannot say which time is wrong: a gap of about 1 h 17 min at the start of the raw recording that the file drops, and a two-hour error in the trial times (a time zone, for example), would fit. Relative times within each clock are consistent, which is what the analysis needs.

From here on, spike times are placed on the trial clock by adding the measured offset. The next cell checks this against the task.

# Contrasts: does each stream respond to the task at V on the trial clock?
rng_check = np.random.default_rng(1)
V = succ.V.to_numpy()
spk_trial = spk + OFFSET
def null_alignments(n, rng):
    """V replaced by a uniform time within each successful trial's span (its start to the next trial's start)."""
    return [rng.uniform(succ.trial_start.to_numpy(), succ.trial_end.to_numpy()) for _ in range(n)]
nulls = null_alignments(100, rng_check)
null_mod = np.array([chamber.modulation(chamber.psth(spk_trial, a)[1]) for a in nulls])
rows = []
for label, extra in [("measured offset", 0.0), ("offset - 5 s", -5.0), ("offset + 5 s", 5.0)]:
    _, c = chamber.psth(spk_trial + extra, V)
    rows.append({"spike clock": label, "modulation": chamber.modulation(c)})
_, c0 = chamber.psth(spk, V)
rows.append({"spike clock": "as stored (no offset)", "modulation": chamber.modulation(c0),
             })
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# LFP: evoked potential at V against random times in the same trials.
def evoked_raw(times, pad=1.0):
    out = []
    for t0 in times:
        k = np.searchsorted(lfp_t, t0 - pad)
        seg = lfp_v[k:k + 2001]
        if len(seg) == 2001 and not np.isnan(seg).any():
            out.append(seg - seg[:1000].mean())
    return np.array(out)
ev_true = evoked_raw(V)
ev_null = [evoked_raw(a) for a in nulls[:30]]
amp = lambda e: np.ptp(e.mean(0)[1000:1500])
print(f"\nLFP: peak-to-peak of the mean LFP 0-0.5 s after V, {len(ev_true)} trials: {amp(ev_true) * 1e6:.1f} uV; "
      f"random times in the same trials, 95th percentile {np.percentile([amp(e) for e in ev_null], 95) * 1e6:.1f} uV")

# Dopamine: when do large and small trials diverge, relative to V?
t_da, da_al = chamber.dopamine_aligned(fscv, succ)
big = (succ.reward == "large").to_numpy()
tt = stats.ttest_ind(da_al[big], da_al[~big], nan_policy="omit").statistic
tt = np.asarray(tt)
run = np.convolve(np.abs(tt) > 3, np.ones(5, int), "valid") == 5
first = t_da[np.argmax(run)] if run.any() else None
print(f"\nDopamine: first time from V at which |t| (large against small) exceeds 3 for 5 samples running: {first:.1f} s;"
      f" largest |t| before V: {np.nanmax(np.abs(tt[t_da < 0])):.2f}")

as stored (no offset)        0.01           0.06
Successful trials with V inside the stored spike times' range: 399 of 951

LFP: peak-to-peak of the mean LFP 0-0.5 s after V, 951 trials: 18.6 uV; random times in the same trials, 95th percentile 3.7 uV

With the measured offset the spike rate is locked to V: the variance of the trial-averaged rate across bins is far above that at random times in the same trials. Moved 5 s later it is not; moved 5 s earlier it is still above chance, as the window then holds the time of the reward, about 4.8 s after V. As stored it is not. As stored, V falls within the range of the spike times in only 399 of 951 successful trials. This contrast places the spikes on the task to within a few seconds (the response is broad, so smaller shifts keep a high variance); the millisecond alignment rests on the two steps above.

The LFP shows an evoked potential after V larger than at random times in the same trials, and the dopamine of large and small trials diverges only after V (from 2.5 s), with no run of |t| above 3 before it (largest 2.06). Both are consistent with the LFP and the FSCV table sharing the trial clock, as their construction from the trials' start times implies.

The raw FSCV holds 196800 scans placed back to back at 10 Hz from the first trial's start, 328 min in all, longer than the 302 min of trials, so the minute files were joined without their gaps; the conversion sets only a starting time. The current is stated in amperes but its values (around 1000) are nA. The trial-aligned oxidation current cannot be found in it: the best lags differ from trial to trial and their correlations are no better than the 30th best. The raw FSCV's clock could therefore not be established. No claim uses the raw FSCV.

No recording is deposited twice. The thresholded spikes and the Plexon unit are two sortings of the same channel; the analysis uses the thresholded file, which is the one in the paper's data record.

In a single trial (trial 133 of the session), dopamine concentration changes at site c8ds fluctuate, especially after the value cue display.

Result: reproduced, on weak evidence. In trial 133 (1-based, a successful large reward trial) the SD of dopamine over the 5 s after V is 2.02 times that over the 5 s before; under the other reading (index 133, trial 134) the ratio is 2.04, with 36% and 46% of its samples NaN. The test says little: of the 889 successful trials with a reference at V, the median ratio is 1.27, 64% are above 1, and trial 133's ratio is above 76.9% of them. The criterion was also written after trial 133's values had been printed (see the claims file).

fig8b-dopamine-large-vs-small¶

Trial-averaged dopamine at site c8ds, aligned to the value cue, increases more for large than for small reward trials, especially between the value cue display and reward.

Criterion: per successful trial, mean dopamine (referenced at V) from V to RW; large above small, two-sided Mann-Whitney p < 0.05.

In [12]:
def window_by_trial(da, t_axis, lo, hi):
    """Mean of each row between per-trial bounds lo[i] and hi[i] (s from V)."""
    out = np.full(len(da), np.nan)
    for i in range(len(da)):
        m = (t_axis >= lo[i]) & (t_axis <= hi[i])
        if np.any(~np.isnan(da[i, m])):
            out[i] = np.nanmean(da[i, m])
    return out
rw = (succ.RW - succ.V).to_numpy()
main = window_by_trial(da_al, t_da, np.zeros(len(succ)), rw)
def compare(values, mask_big, label):
    a, b = values[mask_big], values[~mask_big]
    a, b = a[~np.isnan(a)], b[~np.isnan(b)]
    p = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided").pvalue
    d = (a.mean() - b.mean()) / np.sqrt((a.var(ddof=1) + b.var(ddof=1)) / 2)
    return {"window": label, "n_large": len(a), "n_small": len(b), "mean_large": a.mean(), "mean_small": b.mean(),
            "difference": a.mean() - b.mean(), "cohen_d": d, "mann_whitney_p": p}
rows = [compare(main, big, "V to RW (main)")]
print("Dropped (no dopamine sample in V to RW): large", int(np.isnan(main[big]).sum()), ", small", int(np.isnan(main[~big]).sum()))
rows.append(compare(window_by_trial(da_al, t_da, np.zeros(len(succ)), np.full(len(succ), 2.0)), big, "0 to 2 s"))
rows.append(compare(window_by_trial(da_al, t_da, rw, rw + 3), big, "RW to RW + 3 s"))
rows.append(compare(window_by_trial(da_al, t_da, np.full(len(succ), -3.0), np.zeros(len(succ))), big, "-3 to 0 s (before V)"))
half = (succ.trial <= len(trials) / 2).to_numpy()
for name, m in (("first half of session", half), ("second half of session", ~half)):
    r = compare(main[m], big[m], "V to RW")
    r["window"] = f"V to RW, {name}"
    rows.append(r)
keep = (succ.trial != 1411).to_numpy()
r = compare(main[keep], big[keep], "V to RW")
r["window"] = "V to RW, without trial 1411"
rows.append(r)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
# Trials are not independent: dopamine drifts across the session. Labels shuffled within blocks of 50
# consecutive successful trials keep the drift in the null.
rng_8b = np.random.default_rng(8)

Result: reproduced. From V to reward, dopamine referenced at V is higher in large than in small reward trials (means 1.88 against 1.10, difference 0.78 in the file's unstated unit, Cohen's d 0.19, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0035; 429 and 460 trials, 23 and 39 dropped for lack of a reference at V). Shuffling the labels only within blocks of 50 consecutive trials, which keeps the drift across the session in the null, gives p = 0.0045. The difference is small in the first 2 s after V (p = 0.44) and largest after reward (RW to RW + 3 s, difference 1.59, p = 0.0001, within blocks p = 0.0010), and the two conditions do not differ before V (p = 0.50). It holds in the second half of the session (p = 0.0125) and not significantly in the first (p = 0.075). Without trial 1411, p = 0.0031.

fig9a-spikes-task-aligned¶

Spikes recorded at site c5d on a chamber-implanted CFE can be shown as a raster and a peristimulus time histogram aligned to the value cue display, for large and small reward trials.

Criterion: (i) at least 90% of successful trials have a spike within V-1 s to V+3 s; (ii) the variance across 100 ms bins of the PSTH exceeds the 95th percentile of 200 random alignments within the same trials. Spike times on the trial clock with the offset measured in the data check.

Result: reproduced, after the spike times are moved to the trial clock. With the offset measured in the data check, every successful trial has a spike within V - 1 s to V + 3 s, and the bin variance of the PSTH is 0.49 against a 95th percentile of 0.06 for random alignments (p = 0.005 with 200 alignments); with the 7 ms lag also corrected it is 0.48, and the Plexon unit gives 0.17 against 0.06. The rate falls from 5.63 spikes/s before V to 4.58 in the first 0.2 s after it (lowest bin 3.54 spikes/s at 0.25 s in large trials) and rises to 7.70 at 0.3 to 0.5 s, peaking at 0.45 s for large trials (8.5 spikes/s) and 0.35 s for small (8.0). Large and small trials do not differ over 0 to 1 s (5.69 against 5.66 spikes/s, p = 0.90). With the spike times as stored, only 42% of trials have a spike in the window and the variance is 0.01 against 0.03, so the claim fails on the file as published.

fig9bc-unit-waveform-isi¶

The spikes at site c5d have a consistent waveform (mean and standard deviation) and an interspike interval distribution (1 ms bins) consistent with a single unit.

Criterion: fewer than 1% of ISIs below 1 ms, and the largest absolute value of the mean waveform more than twice the SD across spikes at that sample.

Result: reproduced by the criterion, but the evidence for a single unit is weak. No ISI is shorter than 1 ms, and the mean waveform's trough (-56.4 µV) is 4.79 times the SD across spikes at that sample. Neither part could easily fail. The shortest ISI, 1.562 ms, just exceeds the 48-sample (1.50 ms) waveform, so the detector's dead time excludes ISIs under 1 ms; and every one of the 101733 spikes exceeds the 40 µV threshold (smallest peak 40.3 µV), which nearly forces the mean trough above twice the SD. Above the dead time, ISIs are rarer than at longer intervals (per ms, 0.106 times as many at 1.56 to 3 ms as at 10 to 30 ms; Plexon unit 0.204), which fits a refractory period in most spikes but does not rule out spikes of other units. The two sortings differ: only 54411 of the Plexon unit's 90912 spikes lie within 0.2 ms of a spike of thresholded unit 1, which has 101733. The Plexon unit has 1 ISI under 1 ms, 14 (0.015%) under 1.56 ms and 39 (0.04%) under 2 ms.

fig9d-beta-suppression-large¶

Trial-averaged beta-band LFP power at c7b referenced to c5c is suppressed more in the brief window after the value cue for large than for small reward cues.

Criterion: per successful trial, log10 of mean 13-30 Hz power over 0 to 0.5 s after V divided by the 0.5 s before V; large lower than small, two-sided Mann-Whitney p < 0.05.

In [15]:
def beta_test(band, post, base, label):
    t_ax, pw = chamber.band_power_around(lfp_t, lfp_v, V, band=band)
    ratio = np.log10(chamber.window_mean(t_ax, pw, *post) / chamber.window_mean(t_ax, pw, *base))
    a, b = ratio[big], ratio[~big]
    dropped = (int(np.isnan(a).sum()), int(np.isnan(b).sum()))
    a, b = a[~np.isnan(a)], b[~np.isnan(b)]
    p = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided").pvalue
    w_a, w_b = stats.wilcoxon(a).pvalue, stats.wilcoxon(b).pvalue
    return {"variant": label, "n_large": len(a), "n_small": len(b), "dropped (l, s)": dropped,
            "median_large": np.median(a), "median_small": np.median(b), "diff_medians": np.median(a) - np.median(b),
            "mann_whitney_p": p, "p large != 0": w_a, "p small != 0": w_b}, t_ax, pw
rows = []
r, t_beta, pw_beta = beta_test((13, 30), (0, 0.5), (-0.5, 0), "13-30 Hz, 0-0.5 s vs 0.5 s before (main)")
rows.append(r)
for band, post, base, label in [((13, 30), (0, 0.3), (-0.5, 0), "post 0-0.3 s"), ((13, 30), (0, 1.0), (-0.5, 0), "post 0-1 s"),
                                ((13, 30), (0, 0.5), (-1.0, 0), "1 s baseline"), ((15, 30), (0, 0.5), (-0.5, 0), "15-30 Hz"),
                                ((12, 25), (0, 0.5), (-0.5, 0), "12-25 Hz")]:
    rows.append(beta_test(band, post, base, label)[0])
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))

      f"Mann-Whitney p = {stats.mannwhitneyu(raw_post[big & ok], raw_post[~big & ok]).pvalue:.3g}")

Result: partially reproduced. Beta power (13 to 30 Hz) falls after V in both conditions (median log10 ratio -0.158 for large and -0.125 for small, each p < 0.001 against 0), and the fall is larger for large reward cues, but not significantly (difference of medians -0.033, Mann-Whitney p = 0.108; shuffling within blocks of 50 trials, p = 0.19). Averaged over trials, as in the paper's figure, power over 0 to 0.5 s is 0.839 of the baseline for large (95% CI 0.782 to 0.903) and 0.885 for small (0.831 to 0.940), a difference of -0.046 (-0.125 to 0.036). No variant reaches p < 0.05: 15 to 30 Hz gives p = 0.063, a 1 s baseline p = 0.108, and the 0 to 0.3 s and 0 to 1 s windows show no difference (p = 0.59 and 0.84). The plot stops at ±1.5 s, as the filter's edge effects distort the last samples of each 6 s segment (normalized power 0.16 to 0.32 at ±3 s); the test windows lie within ±1 s.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper gives no analysis methods for Figures 8 and 9 beyond the alignment to V and the background subtraction at V. The windows, the beta band (13 to 30 Hz), the power measure, the tests and the ISI and waveform criteria are choices made here and fixed in the claims file. Dopamine is referenced at V by subtracting the PCA estimate at V, which equals background subtraction at V when the PCA model is linear; where dopamine is NaN at V, the reference is interpolated across the gap when valid samples lie within 0.2 s on both sides, and the trial is dropped otherwise. The tests treat trials as independent; shuffling within blocks of 50 consecutive trials, shown as a variant, does not change the outcomes. The spike times are moved by the offset measured in the data check (11812.11 s). Trial 1411, which the paper's large reward list leaves out, is kept.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • The raw ephys and the spike times are not on the clock of the trials, events, LFP and FSCV table. The raw ephys is stored from 0 s with no timestamps; locating it in the stored LFP puts it at 11812.11 s, with a drift of about 4 ms per hour. Without this correction the spike claim fails. The dandiset description says all data are expressed relative to the start of the Neuralynx recording, which the data contradict.
  • The absolute times disagree: on the trial clock the raw samples end at 17:12:20, two hours after the recording-closed time in the Neuralynx header (15:12:24).
  • The stored spike times are about 7.1 ms after the spike troughs in raw c5d.
  • The "beta-band LFP" is broadband, its values are already volts, and it carries the raw int16 conversion factor. The thresholded waveforms are stated in volts but hold µV; the raw FSCV current is stated in amperes but holds nA. The trial-aligned FSCV columns state no units.
  • The subject description, session and experiment descriptions and one keyword describe the lab's micro-invasive probe study, not this paper.
  • The event table repeats each event once per overlapping 60 s trial window (about five copies on average: 7221 stored trial-start events for 1412 distinct ones; unsorted). The trial tags carry no trial type; reward size and outcome come from the events, and they reproduce the paper's trial lists.
  • The Plexon unit's spike times are not sorted.
  • The raw FSCV minute files are joined without their gaps (328 min against 302 min of trials), and the trial-aligned oxidation current cannot be found in them, so the raw FSCV's clock could not be established.
  • Raw c5c sits at the input range in about 1.7% of samples, and the raw signals carry a large 10 Hz artefact (the FSCV scan rate).
  • The reward size is said to depend on whether the target is at the top or bottom of the screen; the events code left and right conditions, which do not predict reward size.
  • Only monkey T and one session are deposited; the data behind the yield, culture, drainage and bone-growth results are not.
